description: A bình thủy: a tin-and-glass thermos printed with peach blossoms, from the Rạng Đông factory.  Every household fills one with boiling water in the morning for tea all day.
A squat unglazed clay pot blackened by charcoal, the only proper vessel for cá kho tộ: fish braised in caramel and fish sauce until the sauce turns sticky.
A thick round slice of tamarind trunk, the thớt gỗ me every kitchen chops on.  The cleaver has worn a dip in the middle after years of daily use.
A chổi chà: a stiff bundle of coconut leaf ribs bound to a short bamboo handle, for sweeping the sidewalk out front at dawn.
A dented aluminium kettle, sooty on the bottom from the honeycomb-coal stove, for boiling water for tea and the vacuum flask.
A dome of woven plastic mesh in pink or green, set over the dishes on the table to keep the flies off until the family sits down.

The roadside tyre mender's kit: tyre levers, rubber patches cut from old inner tubes, glue, sandpaper and a basin of water to find the leak.  Every few blocks a man with this kit and a hand pump waited under a tree for punctures.
A long, light bamboo pole with nylon line, a float cut from a flip-flop and a small hook, for fishing the canals and the ponds of the outskirts.
A heavy hardened-steel khóa chữ U, the lock every Saigon rider clamps through the front wheel at night.  Swung by the shackle, it is a short, brutal club.

An olive-green pith helmet of pressed fibre under cloth, with a red star badge, worn by veterans, cyclo drivers, construction workers and old men reading the paper.  It keeps the sun off the head and neck.
A matching shirt and trousers of thin flowered rayon, the loose home clothes Saigon women wear all day: at home, at the market and on the motorbike.
A black-and-white checked cotton scarf from the Mekong Delta, knotted round the neck against the sun or wrapped over the face against road dust.
Sandals with a strap behind the heel, so they stay on when you run for the bus or wade a flooded street: the school and office shoe of the south.
